prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN)  -- Far too many passengers are being stranded on board commercial flights in the United States in delays, an air passengers' rights group said Wednesday. Delta Air Lines, JetBlue, Continental Airlines, and US Airways received an overall grade of "F" on the air travel consumer report card. FlyersRights.org, in issuing what it calls an air travel consumer report card, said there were more than 1,200 tarmac strandings -- in which passengers are locked in planes on the runways -- in 2008. Delta Air Lines had the greatest number of tarmac delays longer than three hours. Southwest Airlines was rated the best for handling delays by letting customers get off delayed planes, as well as providing food, water and other items. The longest delay the organization found was a January 2008 Delta flight from Atlanta, Georgia, to Florida, in which passengers waited on the tarmac for more than 10 hours without food and water. "Too many Americans have been locked inside sealed airplanes, trapped in tubes on the tarmac, for three hours or more," said FlyersRights.org Executive Director Kate Hanni. "It's time for Congress to give airline passengers the legal right to get off planes stuck on the ground for three hours or more." Hanni -- who has been lobbying for an airline passengers' bill of rights -- also said America's economic situation has exacerbated the problems consumers face on the airlines because of layoffs. "Airlines are trying to maintain or increase their profit margins," she said. "They have decreased all of their goods and services related to flying." She added that a timely flight is "not just a matter of passenger convenience, it's a matter of public safety." "I wonder if heroic Captain Chesley 'Sully' Sullenberger and his crew could have performed as they did after seven, nine or even 12 hours on the tarmac?" Hanni asked, making a reference to the US Airways crew that made an emergency landing in New York's Hudson River in January. Hanni started her organization after she was stranded on the tarmac on an American Airlines flight in Austin, Texas, for more than nine hours in December 2006. Mark Mogel, the group's research director, said FlyersRights.org has about 24,000 members, many of whom donate money, services and lobbying help. The report card is based on government statistics, press reports, airline Web site data, reports on the group's hotline, and eyewitness accounts from January to December of 2008. It surveyed 17 airlines for various kinds of tarmac delays, their menu and contracts of carriage and customer service commitments and issued grades for these separate factors and an overall grade. As for the menu, Mogel specified that the menu grade is based on quantity, not quality. The survey was looking to see whether there would be food on board during a tarmac delay. Delta Air Lines, JetBlue, Continental Airlines, and US Airways received an overall grade of "F" and American Airlines received an overall grade of "D." United Airlines, Airtran and American Eagle got a "C." Alaska Airlines, Northwest Airlines and Frontier Airlines got a "B," and Southwest received an "A." Five other airlines -- Atlantic Southeast, Comair, ExpressJet, Mesa and Pinnacle -- didn't get an overall grade because some categories couldn't be completed. "The fact that some airlines have received A's and B's and others D's and F's on this report card also shows that providing decent customer service and avoidance of strandings is both achievable and should not place an undue burden on the airline industry or lead to higher ticket prices," the report's executive summary said. CNN's Joe Sterling contributed to this report.

She added that a timely flight is “not just a matter of passenger convenience, it’s a matter of public safety.”

“I wonder if heroic Captain Chesley ‘Sully’ Sullenberger and his crew could have performed as they did after seven, nine or even 12 hours on the tarmac?” Hanni asked, referring to the US Airways crew that made an emergency landing in New York’s Hudson River in January.

Hanni founded her organization after she was stranded on the tarmac aboard an American Airlines flight in Austin, Texas, for more than nine hours in December 2006.

The report card was based on government statistics, press reports, airline website data, reports submitted through the group’s hotline and eyewitness accounts collected from January through December 2008.

It evaluated 17 airlines on various types of tarmac delays, their menus, contracts of carriage and customer service commitments, assigning grades for each category as well as an overall grade.

(CNN) — A U.S. airline-passenger advocacy organization said Wednesday that commercial carriers are leaving far too many travelers confined aboard aircraft during lengthy delays.

FlyersRights.org released what it describes as an air-travel consumer report card, giving Delta Air Lines, JetBlue, Continental Airlines and US Airways overall failing grades. According to the organization, more than 1,200 incidents occurred in 2008 in which passengers were kept inside planes while they remained on the tarmac. Delta recorded the highest number of ground delays lasting longer than three hours.

Southwest Airlines earned the top rating for its response to delays. The group said Southwest allowed travelers to leave delayed aircraft and supplied food, water and other necessities.

The most severe case identified in the report involved a Delta flight scheduled to travel from Atlanta, Georgia, to Florida in January 2008. Passengers reportedly spent more than 10 hours on the tarmac without food or water.

FlyersRights.org Executive Director Kate Hanni said an excessive number of Americans have been confined in sealed aircraft for at least three hours. She urged Congress to establish a legal right allowing passengers to leave planes that have remained on the ground for three hours or longer.

Hanni, who has been campaigning for an airline passengers’ bill of rights, said layoffs associated with the nation’s economic conditions have made travelers’ problems worse. In her view, airlines seeking to preserve or expand profit margins have reduced the products and services connected with air travel.

She also argued that on-time operations concern public safety, not merely passenger comfort. Referring to the US Airways crew that carried out an emergency landing in New York’s Hudson River in January, Hanni questioned whether Capt. Chesley “Sully” Sullenberger and his crew could have performed so successfully after spending seven, nine or even 12 hours waiting on the tarmac.

Hanni founded FlyersRights.org after being stuck for more than nine hours on an American Airlines plane in Austin, Texas, in December 2006.

The organization’s research director, Mark Mogel, said the group has approximately 24,000 members. Many contribute money, professional services or assistance with lobbying.

The report evaluated 17 airlines using information covering January through December 2008. Its sources included government data, media coverage, material from airline websites, calls to the organization’s hotline and firsthand witness accounts. Airlines were assessed on several types of tarmac delays, onboard menus, contracts of carriage and customer-service promises. Grades were assigned in each category as well as overall.

Mogel explained that the menu score measured the amount of food available rather than its quality. The review focused on whether food would be aboard an aircraft during a tarmac delay.

Delta, JetBlue, Continental and US Airways each received an overall “F,” while American Airlines was awarded a “D.” United Airlines, AirTran and American Eagle earned “C” grades. Alaska Airlines, Northwest Airlines and Frontier Airlines received “B” ratings, and Southwest was given an “A.”

No overall score was issued for five other carriers—Atlantic Southeast, Comair, ExpressJet, Mesa and Pinnacle—because the organization lacked enough information to complete certain categories.

In its executive summary, the report said the range of results—from “A” and “B” ratings to “D” and “F” grades—demonstrates that airlines can provide acceptable customer service and prevent passengers from being stranded without imposing an unreasonable burden on the industry or increasing ticket prices.

CNN’s Joe Sterling contributed to the report.

counterfactuals.output:
# FlyersRights report card puts airlines on notice over long tarmac delays

**By CNN-style staff report**

Airline passengers spent far too much time trapped on grounded planes in 2008, according to a consumer report card released by FlyersRights.org, which used letter grades to highlight sharp differences among U.S. carriers.

The passenger advocacy group’s review focused heavily on flights that remained on the tarmac for three hours or longer — delays that can leave travelers confined inside aircraft with limited access to food, water and working restrooms.

FlyersRights.org said the problem underscored the need for enforceable passenger protections rather than voluntary airline policies. The organization called for rules requiring carriers to provide basic necessities during extended delays and to give passengers an opportunity to leave an aircraft after a specified period, when safety and security permit.

The report card graded airlines using federal transportation data and other measures of customer service, including lengthy ground delays, on-time performance, baggage handling, complaints and involuntary denied boardings. Carriers with fewer serious disruptions and stronger overall service received higher marks, while airlines with repeated long-delay incidents fell toward the bottom of the rankings, with some receiving failing grades.

The group cautioned that an airline’s overall grade did not guarantee an individual passenger a trouble-free trip. Weather, airport congestion and air traffic control restrictions can affect every carrier. But FlyersRights.org argued that airline decisions — including scheduling, staffing and how quickly a plane returns to a gate — often determine whether a disruption becomes an hours-long ordeal.

Lengthy tarmac delays had become a national consumer issue after several highly publicized incidents in which passengers were kept aboard aircraft for extended periods. FlyersRights.org grew out of that frustration and pressed Congress and the Department of Transportation to adopt an “airline passenger bill of rights.”

Airlines have generally maintained that rigid time limits could lead to more flight cancellations and complicate operations during severe weather. Passenger advocates counter that travelers should not be forced to remain indefinitely on planes without clear information or essential services.

For FlyersRights.org, the 2008 grades were intended as both a guide for consumers and a warning to the industry: Airlines should be judged not only by ticket prices and departure times, but also by how they treat passengers when a flight stops moving.

## FlyersRights.org urges Congress to guarantee escape from planes after three-hour ground delays

**WASHINGTON —** FlyersRights.org is calling on Congress to require airlines to let passengers leave aircraft that have been sitting on the ground for three hours, arguing that voluntary industry promises have failed to prevent travelers from being trapped for prolonged periods without adequate food, water or working restrooms.

Kate Hanni, the organization’s founder and executive director, said passengers should not have to depend on an airline’s discretion once a ground delay reaches three hours.

“Three hours is enough,” Hanni said, describing the proposal as “an issue of basic human rights.”

Under the policy advocated by FlyersRights.org, an airline would have to return a delayed aircraft to a gate or provide another safe way for passengers to disembark after three hours. Exceptions could be made when the pilot determines that moving the aircraft would create a genuine safety or security risk.

The proposal would not require a flight to be canceled at the three-hour mark. Airlines could allow passengers who wished to remain aboard to do so, while giving others the opportunity to leave. The group said the essential point is that travelers should not be confined indefinitely because an airline hopes a departure slot will open.

Hanni, who became an advocate after being stranded aboard an American Airlines flight for hours in Austin, Texas, said airlines had repeatedly demonstrated that voluntary customer-service commitments were inadequate. She argued that delays caused by weather or congestion do not justify keeping people inside a stationary aircraft without a meaningful choice.

“This is not about preventing delays,” Hanni said. “It is about preventing passengers from being held on airplanes for hours with no way to get off.”

### Seventeen airlines receive failing grades

To reinforce its case, FlyersRights.org issued a report card grading 17 U.S. airlines on whether their policies gave passengers an enforceable right to leave after a three-hour ground delay. The organization awarded an **F to every carrier**, saying none provided the firm, passenger-controlled guarantee it was seeking.

The grades were:

| Airline | Grade |
|---|---:|
| AirTran Airways | F |
| Alaska Airlines | F |
| American Airlines | F |
| American Eagle | F |
| Atlantic Southeast Airlines | F |
| Comair | F |
| Continental Airlines | F |
| Delta Air Lines | F |
| ExpressJet Airlines | F |
| Frontier Airlines | F |
| Hawaiian Airlines | F |
| JetBlue Airways | F |
| Northwest Airlines | F |
| SkyWest Airlines | F |
| Southwest Airlines | F |
| United Airlines | F |
| US Airways | F |

The organization said the uniformly poor marks did not necessarily mean that every airline handled delays in the same way. Rather, the grades reflected the absence of a clear, binding rule requiring deplaning after three hours. Policies that merely promised food, water, updates or efforts to return to a gate did not qualify for a passing grade if the airline retained complete discretion over when passengers could leave.

FlyersRights.org argued that even carriers with relatively strong customer-service plans could change those plans without meaningful consequences. A federal law, Hanni said, would establish a consistent national standard and make the three-hour limit enforceable.

### Pressure for federal action

The campaign followed a series of highly publicized incidents in which passengers spent many hours aboard aircraft waiting to take off or reach a gate. Travelers in some cases reported overflowing toilets, inadequate ventilation, limited drinking water and scarce information from airline crews.

Airlines have generally opposed rigid time limits, warning that a mandatory return to the gate could lead to more canceled flights. They also contend that severe weather, crowded airports and instructions from air-traffic controllers can leave pilots with few workable options.

FlyersRights.org responded that operational inconvenience should not outweigh passengers’ health and liberty. The group said carriers would have a strong incentive to improve scheduling, gate access and contingency planning if they knew they could no longer keep travelers aboard indefinitely.

The organization urged lawmakers to make the three-hour deplaning requirement part of a broader airline-passenger bill of rights. In addition to the right to leave a delayed plane, the group sought reliable access to food, potable water, functioning toilets, medical assistance and timely information during extended disruptions.

For Hanni, the central issue was straightforward: Airlines may control whether and when an aircraft departs, but after three hours on the ground, passengers should control whether they remain aboard.

**Passengers push for stronger protections as lengthy tarmac delays persist**

**By CNN Staff**

Long waits aboard grounded aircraft are again drawing scrutiny from passenger advocates, who say travelers need stronger protections when flights remain stuck on the tarmac for hours.

Kate Hanni, founder of the Coalition for an Airline Passengers’ Bill of Rights, has been a leading voice in that campaign. Her advocacy began after she and her family were stranded aboard an American Airlines flight in Austin, Texas, for more than nine hours in December 2006. Passengers were unable to leave the aircraft and faced dwindling food, water and working restroom facilities, Hanni has said.

The experience prompted her to press Congress and federal regulators for an airline passengers’ bill of rights, including enforceable limits on tarmac delays and requirements that carriers provide food, water, functioning restrooms and medical assistance.

Federal rules now generally prohibit U.S. airlines from keeping passengers on the tarmac for more than three hours on domestic flights and four hours on international flights without allowing them to deplane, although safety, security and air-traffic-control exceptions apply. Airlines also must provide food and water after two hours and ensure that restrooms remain operational.

Still, advocates say enforcement and airline performance remain uneven. In passenger-focused assessments, carriers have received grades spanning the full traditional range — **A, B, C, D and F** — reflecting sharp differences in delay records, customer service and treatment of stranded travelers.

Airlines have argued that severe weather, airport congestion and air-traffic-control restrictions can make delays unavoidable. Hanni and other advocates counter that passengers should not be left confined indefinitely, regardless of the cause.

“No traveler should have to endure what happened to us in 2006,” Hanni has said in describing the campaign. “Passengers deserve basic rights when an airline keeps them on board.”
